tip: 'Faire' + infinitive = make someone do something: 'fais-moi penser à acheter du pain' is literally 'make me think to buy bread' – remind me to buy bread.
'Certes... mais' = 'admittedly... but': you concede the point, then counter it, as in 'certes, c'est difficile, mais pas impossible'.
'Je me suis fait voler' isn't 'I made someone steal' – 'se faire' + infinitive marks something done TO you: I had my phone stolen.
'Il m'a été impossible' is literally 'it to-me was impossible' – that 'm'' names who couldn't do it: I couldn't reach her.
French usually skips the passive for theft: 'on m'a volé mon portefeuille' is literally 'they stole me my wallet.' The 'm'' marks who got robbed, not who did it.
For 'about to,' French uses 'aller' in the imperfect: 'ils allaient partir' means 'they were about to leave' – not 'they used to leave.'
That 'ne' isn't a 'not': after 'à moins que', French drops in a decorative 'ne'. 'Vous ne changiez d'avis' still means 'you change your mind,' not 'you don't.'
'D'autant plus que' = 'especially since', 'all the more because': 'd'autant plus qu'il est malade' = especially since he's sick.
'Toutefois' = however. Slightly more formal than 'cependant'. Used in written French.
'Si bien que' = 'so that' or 'with the result that' – and it takes the normal verb form, not the subjunctive.
'Faire' + infinitive: the subject causes the action but doesn't do it – 'nous faisons repeindre' = we're having it repainted, someone else paints.
At the start of a clause 'aussi' flips from 'also' to 'therefore' – and the verb swaps in front of the subject: 'aussi a-t-il décidé'. Mid-sentence it's plain 'also' again.
French has no '-ing' tense. To stress an action happening right now, use 'être en train de' + verb: 'est en train de dormir' = is in the middle of sleeping.
French slang borrows the English word 'speed' as an adjective meaning wired or hyper: 'il est trop speed' = he's too wound up. Nothing to do with velocity.
'Venir de' (to have just done) in the past tense gives 'had just': 'nous venions de nous installer' = we had just settled in.
In a reported question 'what' becomes 'ce que', not 'qu'est-ce que': 'nous a demandé ce que nous voulions' – word order stays normal, unlike a direct question.
To report a negative command, put 'de ne pas' before the verb: 'de ne pas faire de bruit' = not to make noise.
'Conseiller' slips in a 'de' before the infinitive that English simply omits: 'conseillé de me reposer' = advised me to rest.
'Bien que' (although) takes the subjunctive: 'bien qu'il soit fatigué' = although he is tired – 'soit', not 'est'.
'Demander de' + verb turns a command into reported speech: 'Range ta chambre !' becomes 'ma mère m'a demandé de ranger ma chambre'.
'En dépit de' = despite. More formal than 'malgré'. Both take a noun, not a clause.
'En revanche' = on the other hand. Used for contrasting two facts. More formal than 'par contre'.
'Force est de' + verb is a formal 'one must acknowledge': 'force est de constater' = we have to admit.
French has no '-ing' tense. To pin an action to right now, wrap it in 'être en train de': 'est en train d'atterrir' = is in the middle of landing this very second.
'Finir par' isn't about finishing – it means to end up doing something eventually: 'vont finir par accepter' = they'll come around to accepting in the end.
'A filé à l'anglaise' = slipped away without saying goodbye, literally 'English-style'. English flips it round: 'to take French leave'.
'Laisser tomber' is literally 'to let fall', but it means to drop or quit: 'a laissé tomber ses études' = gave up his studies. Also how you say you ditched someone.
'Je viens de finir' means 'I just finished' – 'venir de' + verb is French's recent past. It reads literally as 'I come from finishing', yet the plain present does past-tense work here.
A reported yes/no question uses 'si' where a direct one used 'est-ce que': 'elle m'a demandé si j'avais faim' = she asked if I was hungry.
'Se faire' + verb = get something done to you: 'je me suis fait couper les cheveux' = I got my hair cut (someone else cut it).
